analysis.one_liner: Bans workers under 18 from handling tobacco plants or leaves.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote; it sat in the Education and Workforce Committee until the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal child labor law so that anyone under 18 working with tobacco plants or dried tobacco leaves counts as illegal 'oppressive child labor.' That matters because workers absorb nicotine through their skin while handling tobacco, a condition known as green tobacco sickness. The bill was introduced in June 2023 and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, where it stayed until the Congress ended in January 2025 without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Children under 18 who would otherwise work in tobacco fields and curing barns, where direct contact with the plant can cause nicotine poisoning, nausea, and other health harms.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Fair Labor Standards Act to classify work with direct contact with tobacco plants or dried tobacco leaves by anyone under 18 as 'oppressive child labor,' which is generally prohibited under federal law [S2][S3].

The prohibition applies regardless of the usual agricultural exceptions, because the bill adds tobacco-related agriculture to the list of exemptions carved out of the law's parental and small-farm exception [S3].
Tobacco is unusual among crops because workers absorb nicotine through the skin from contact with the plants and cured leaves, which is why the bill targets direct contact specifically [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco growers who currently rely on workers under 18, including family operations, would lose the ability to legally employ them in direct-contact work.

drawbacks.text: The ban reaches even the law's existing exception for children working on their own family's farm in agriculture, so a farm family's own under-18 children could no longer have direct contact with the tobacco crop [S3].

Enforcement would fall on federal labor inspectors and rely on complaints, and small farms may face compliance questions about what counts as 'direct contact' with tobacco plants or dried leaves [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case for the bill is strong — nicotine exposure through the skin is a well-documented hazard unique to tobacco work — and the cost is limited to a single crop's reliance on young workers. The main fair objection is that the ban covers even family farm children, which some see as federal overreach into family operations, though supporters argue nicotine exposure is dangerous regardless of who employs the child.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on June 12, 2023, with Reps. Payne and Norton as original sponsors [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day, which was the only action it ever received [S1][S5].
The bill never advanced past committee before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco growers who employ or would employ workers under 18 are better off, since the restriction was never enacted; no one else gained from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Growers relying on under-18 tobacco labor

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban under-18 work in direct contact with tobacco.

for.name: Reps. Donald Payne and Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.what_they_did: Joined as original sponsors at introduction.

for.name: 25 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, all Democrats.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-NC)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-led committee took no action on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: Growers would lose the option of employing workers under 18 in direct contact with the crop. Their interest in keeping that labor pool available runs against the health protection the bill offered to child workers.

Manufacturers buy leaf from farms and would face no direct rule, but their supply chain depends on farm labor practices, and a ban on child workers would raise leaf costs at the margin. Their interest in cheap leaf runs against protections for the children doing the harvesting.
